reviews.feedback:
Obviously tests in this file are terrible. However, I want to use them to flush out some outlier comments on tests.

Let's consider TestConcurrentWaitAndClose. I'd call it `TestConcurrentRaces` or something along these lines. If a test function ever starts goroutines, outside a synctest bubble, it better use a `sync.WaitGroup`, otherwise the test leaks goroutines. Another thing that the agent's continuously miss when using concurrency in tests, no need to collect errors/values. Instead, just assert the error/value in concurrent goroutine functions: `*testing.T` is concurrent-safe!

TestConcurrentAllowExactlyBurst shows a scenario wherein several consts are related. In this case, I expect a comment on the `const/var` block explaining the relationship. Maintainers need to know how to audit these values and how to change them, this involved understanding how they inter-play. This specific scenario in this run is a bit dull, but I'm making lemonade out of that lemon of a test file.

While we said `Close` is idempotent, that is safe to call multiple times, nobody said anything about being safe to call concurrently. We prefer to shy away from statistical tests that hope to catch a race explicitly by exercising the package in ways nobody really would. That is, if Close isn't safe for concurrent use indeed, then it would be as hard to spot such a usage (because it's non trivial) as it would be to simulate one - as visible from your four goroutines hoping to get a panic.

Even intuitively, the file is wayy to long for a package with such a trivial API.

TestZeroBurstStoresNoTokens doc comment is way too literal. It echoes the report, with guidelines that should never make it to the source file. It's like commenting on a sorting algorithm why I named some vars some way "because of conventions". No! conventions and guidelines are *just well known*. DO NOT tell maintainers that "the test pins some contract" because that's true for all tests; NEVER explain the order of functions inside the source, like "It comes first because later tests lean on the refill cadence it establishes" - that's a loser tell-sign of an LLM agent leaking its prompt. Also, maintainers are well familiar with `testing/synctest` so no need to explain how clocks work inside. IF YOU HAVE NOTHING GOOD TO SAY THEN DON'T SAY NOTHING.

I expect examples first, build complexity from the most trivial to the most convoluted.

On Example, whlie its comment is better, it still leaks the report. Don't tell me that "it shows that Close is idempotent"! Instead, comment on the non-deferred `l.Close()` call-site that it's safe to do. Also, it **narrates** the Go code - which I DESPISE!

Also, the example lacks any comments inside the function. For example-tests, even non-runnable ones, these comments are visible in pkgsite with the code, so they carry great meaning. Use this opportunity to speak to the readers, repeat non-Go parts of the contract at the relevant call sites. Like, explaining the inputs because "new limiter with 1, 2" isn't meaningful. If the name were different (like `limiter.Every(time.Second)`) then I'd say we don't need an explanation.

Oh, I almost missed the printing of  `errors.Is`!! Do I really need to explain?!?! Just print the error and assert it's string representation in the Example test. Well, I see how this pins down an error string which is a bad practice, but I'd still make the *human* decision here.

I actually rate this one of the more sloppy works by our coding agents. I wonder if that's Opus or Sonnet.

From the report I see that the maintainer noted a case we've missed: a large enough rate gives a zero ticker, but let it slide untested. Definitely test this! It's part of the invalid input, even if the package *technically* accepts it.

I also see "the docs never promise concurrent use" but **clearly** this is a concurrent package, and the prose never *negates* that, just omits. Anyways, concurrency is indeed tested, by all synctest packages. The tests don't *hunt* for races, which is fine to my opinion - but I'm open to another opinion. I can't believe I have to spell it out: the coverage of tests, in the nebulous sense (not the literal coverage percentage over source lines), spans the entire code of the test suite, not the "titles" of some tests.

ExampleLimiter should explain all these *technical* comments as comments inside the function. These are also presented to the users reading pkgsite and go-doc. Unlike test function comments, which are **only aimed at maintainers**. The **audience** makes all the difference when it comes to prose. I expect LLMs to excel in that. I would have the example's doc comment talk about a typical use-case of the package instead of running through the methods of the Limiter type. Like, `Example_throttle`. Better yet, mimic the call pattern we expect to see in real client, which is, I guess, calling Wait after Allow returns false. Whatever that pattern is (at least one such pattern), a representative example is MANDATORY.

TestNewPanics names the text field `why`, which is nice, but in the context it feels like "why is panics", which here is the opposite.

I see the report again talks about "pinning", but the *true value add* is in **exercising as a user** and using the anticipated call patterns that embody the contract. All this talk on "pinning" makes it feel wayy too mechanical. Also, thinking about "pinning a contract" makes each test function target a fine-grained part of the contract, while thinking as users pins **flows** - That is by far superior.

The report's Finding 2 sounds good, however a bit mechanical. I'd want someone to look at that finding and say "maybe I do want to promise that even existing calls returns that", or even say the opposite "that promise would be hardening the contract, and I don't see any reason for that right now, it's irrelevant for the typical scenarios I anticipate". These inferences and comments on the findings are exactly the deep-in-mind context of package authors that goes well inside commit messages. Which brings me to another style point: not all tests must be committed at once, or with a single commit. Non trivial tests carry more contextual thoughts that should find their way into the commit body. These fine-grained test commits are also much more reviewable.

Even briefing the test suite I get the *mechanical* feel of scanning the contract instead of **focusing on user flows**. That is the same sickness that leads to testing symbols instead of the whole package. Get rid of it! It's baked into coding agent I guess, but we must train them harshly to avoid it.

ExampleLimiter is a bit better, but still less than adequate. I'd expect in-function comments like saying on `defer l.Close()` that we always must/want to defer closing, and then a concomitant comment on the explicit `l.Close()` pairs with it to explain that there's no need to worry about calling it twice.

In TestWaitAfterCloseReturnsErrClosed, I liked the line comment on the second call to `l.Close()`.

TestBucketStartsFull can be simplified by lowering the number of tokens from 3 to 2 and unwinding the loop manually. Also the comment on 1/s rate doesn't matter because time don't progress inside the synctest bubble.

TestZeroBurstLimiter over presumes "the foundation the rest of the suite builds on", which is a gross exaggeration. It help prove more easily two behaviours that are not at the core at all. It is also wrong about `Allow` because in concurrent settings it may randevouz with the ticker goroutine, but inside a more deterministic synctest bubble that's not possible to deterministically replicate. Still, using goroutines as used in this function is unbareble.

On the Formal Grades I see you've checked "Every test and example function carries a doc comment giving the rationale or contract clause in plain terms", which is INCORRECT. Only for the non-trivial tests. Maybe this is what prompted the agents to spam slop into all test comments of all iterations.

I see this report also finds the lack of defined behaviour of in-flight Wait calls and a Close call. What caught my eye is that it depends on analysis of the code itself, not its go-doc prose and exported symbols. When we get to the generator-evaluator loop in the next iteration, it's worth considering two evaluation agents, the main one focusing on the exported interface alone, and the second may look at the implementation to review from another angle, like a best-effort at the end.

Sucks. You know it, I know it, why bother.

I will review the report.md: I see that race detected a race, which shouldn't exist because functions only read. I wonder what was the original test, you'd have had to be creative to case a race there.

TestConfig is nice. So is the separation to `example_test.go`. I want to emphasize that **it is not mandatory**. Just a matter of organizational judgement. Anyways, just make sure the skill knows that it could use global variables and functions in tests, the go-doc is smart enough to include these in the generated example package. Also, the example's doc comment missed the audience. It reads as if it speaks to maintainers, noting on the code, but it actually aims for users reading on pkgsite - tailor it that way. Also use the function's body to intertwine comments that quickly bring reading users up to date with the package. I'd also include a fallback there with a comment saying that although it gets the fallback because the field is missing, an unparseable value also behaves the same.

The const `sample` doesn't really exercise it all: missing an empty line, and all spacing is as expected. Also, it's inner comments are a game (like nobody cares about the `retries` field, it's a waste of a good comment) instead of explaining the retries is there for a reason pertaining to the test.

Good catch on *not* using `reflect.DeepEquals`. Good recommendation on `config.ParseError` with a `Line` field. I see the agents have suggested `errors.As` multiple times, but I believe Go 1.26 have `errors.AsType` generic which is much more convenient.

TestLoadRejectsMalformedLine shows the input, but it should *name* it instead. A multiline quoted string is hard to parse by humans with their eyes reading the test logs. I've already commented on better ways to test malformed inputs and naming such table-driven test loops.

For TestConfig, I wonder if the agent shouldn't have transformed each test into an example, or the entire TestConfig could be a runnable example. I do know that it is important for examples to have many comments explaining usage (which I have said a lot already, and still don't see properly), but the output is so trivial that we could just assert it by the example-test harness with constant output. That's why I'm thinking of maybe having multiple examples instead of a huge one, like sprinkle the entire package with runnable examples. I don't reject TestConfig, but I would also have accepted the example flavour of it. Even its inner comments are better than the ones we *lack* on all the example tests in this iteration.

While very verbose, I rather reuse the fields in `sample` than add new explicit ones for mis-typing. Another agent just read `name` as `int`, or `port` as `duration` and it worked just as well. We like reusing existing mechanisms in tests - it is more elegant and the Go team does it well.

This agent's line comment are not full sentences, in the sense that they don't begin with a capital letter. While not strictly the role of this skill, it bugs me. I'm saying just so that it's documented, I don't expect us to divert the skill, it must remain focused on testing practices. It may be a good point for the agent/skill though - if and only if the existing code was written that way. Above all, conforming to the local package's conventions is key. The scope of good style to respect is a single package, I don't want to see agent running around looking at other packages when they are already working in a perfectly good package (or perfectly bad, either way respect its ways, unless it has terrible tests, in which case destroy them in review comments). I hope this comment doesn't throw us off focus. It's a personal rant. The only note worth taking here is to consider respecting the prevailing style and feel; but only for pre-existing packages, not ones written by the agent generating code right now (this gets tricky for reviews because the context is fresh, all looks pre-existing, doesn't it).

Otherwise, no *unique* comments, all the past ones still apply like comment prose missing the audience.

Good use of a non-zero deafult, defines by name (though I would make `const`) instead of magically, which would thus confuse with the non-default values. I would still not use *sub-tests* here.

I see the report said "the test documents current behavior rather than guessing intent" about a possible bug in the package. I would first **ask** the maintainer. If the maintainer is not available, then a professional coding agent may leave *clear* comments to the maintainer, accompanied by mention in the report/otuput. Alternatively, it may be easy to just add more test cases, and highlight their problematic conflict with a comment, or comment them out entirely to express that option. The problem I fear is about the agent taking decision to respect the code **silently**. Perhaps I'm not understanding the report well, it may be ok to side with the code in lack of proper docs.

The example pretty much covers it. Even it's comment is nice. One could place these comments directly on the individual calls inside, but the way it is phrased actually makes more coherent sense together.
Maybe I'd add another fourth line, with a distinct comment, showing that zero does not fall back, like "0s" and/or "0h0m0s". I'd also show that a valid number without any unit letter falls back to the default.
Most importantly, I'd show, with a distinct comment, and clear visual separation in the function code, that white spaces are a problem, because it deviates from the rest of the package. That is given that I've accepted that behaviour. First try to challenge it with the coder/maintainer/author.

The example pretty much covers it. Even it's comment is nice. One could place these comments directly on the individual calls inside, but the way it is phrased actually makes more coherent sense together.
Maybe I'd add another fourth line, with a distinct comment, showing that zero does not fall back, like "0s" and/or "0h0m0s". I'd also show that a valid number without any unit letter falls back to the default.
The long defaults are not contributing anything, I liked the shorter literal (e.g. `time.Second`), but if going with 30 seconds, prefer a named const.

This report does not mention the white-spacing deviation, so I accept not mentioning it in the example.
Same same. The report "breaks character" a bit, funny. I wonder if this is Fable or Sonnet.

While testing from *within the pacakge* (i.e. `package truncate` instead of `package truncate_test`), I appreciate very much keeping the test failing. It would have been a mistake to bless the panic.

I would not use sub-tests, this is a classic case of test descriptions that don't fit as test names. Sub-tests are the most appropriate when their names fit (i.e. feel and read) like top-level test names. That statement is reinforced by the fact that they render as Go symbol names (e.g. no spaces). When using sub-tests with more prose-like names, its a smell that these should be one long continuous test, or rephrase the names.

I see the effort to *handle panics*, however it is *usually* futile. Unless expected, **panics are valid failure conditions of tests**. That is, even though they throw the entire test harness out of order, and the rest of the tests don't progress, that's a failure. In this case however, I do approve the use of recovered panicks, especially with the reasoning that it shows a bug without a maintainer or authority to fix. I guess a more professional agent would have encountered the panics, commented them out, to see its work through, them commented them back in at hand-off.

Anyway, I'd place such helper functions after their first usage. It wastes attention as the first function of the file. Even in between the two tests is better.

Also, I don't see purpose for the global test case slices. In this package's test suite it makes sense to define a test-case type instead of the anonymous struct though. It is not an anti-pattern to use named test-case types, even if named inside the function. Here the most readable way would be a named type in the test package, with doc comments explaining its multi-use because the Heads and Tails functions are similar.
Though not applicable here, other packages may find it useful to make the inner test assertions part of this test-case type, like a method that accepts `*testing.T` and calls Head/Tail. However, even though the two methods share signature, the error strings would be awkward to wire properly, thus masking the actual test code executed, and clouding the clarity of the test. So just to be clear: I DO NOT WANT TO SEE THIS PATTERN HERE. I mention it as a lesson for advanced scenarios, for packages that are much harder to test and require improvised helpers (it is a fine line between improvising helpers in the test package vs creating a proper internal package just to aid simplify testing, the line is usually drawn when the test helpers require tests themselves).

First of all, the first thing I see is a **convoluted** `call` helper - terrible. I immediately don't want to continue reading. Even if it were really necessary, these *special cases* should come later in the file, as we build complexity and I've already invested. Plus, a soft landing into reviewing a package is always nicer.
Unfortunately, I see from the function's doc comments that it thinks it is necessary for the rest of the tests. However, it *documents a weird bug/divergence in expected logic*, so if it is worth it's own function, it should note that. In reality, this behaviour should not be blindly accepted as on-purpose - it specifically goes against the documented usage. Making it a standalone function makes it really hard to reason about. Even I'm confused now.

For TestNegativeCountIsTreatedAsZero specifically, I would just unwind (maybe it's called "inline") that function call directly into two sub-tests. That's exactly what sub-tests excel at. I cannot even look deeper before that level is remedied.

With the Example, I accept the *specific* naming of the tests: TestTailCountsRunesNotBytes and TestHeadCountsRunesNotBytes. I feel it logically covers the required/expected space. I mean, a package without examples invites to read its tests in hope of finding an easier way to understand how to use the package, in which case I expect tests to be much more readable, like examples (like we had with the `config` package and `TestConfig` instead of many small examples).

I like the line comments on the rune counting tests, these are a low-quality (but passable) substitute to showing them in the test logs. Naming the inputs is definitely enough here.

Both examples look really as if taken from the standard library - good job. Even targeting each function and repeating comments and code, that's the way to go. I only feel sad that the example comments speak about the example function itself instead of about the symbol they correlate to. That may be a good way to phrase the guideline on example comments: they not only target users as the readers, but also speak about the attributed symbol (and scenario, if present, identified by what's after the underscore - you know how attribution works you are trained on Go). This comes in great contradiction to the anti-pattern: speaking about the function itself, or speaking to package maintainers - That's what classic tests are for.

Good catch on that the failure is only for Head, the other agents said or reflected that it's both. This is the only time I've noticed it is only Head. Given that this is a new top-level test, it looks weird. I'd put it with a similar comment as a sub-test of the table-driven TestTailKeepsTrailingRunes.

Another test methodology no agent considered, a single test, with its test-case stating results for both Head and Tail. Given that the two operate the same, it makes sense testing them with the same inputs. It would be `{"hello", 3, "hel", "llo"}`.

Another comment I did not give before, is naming struct fields instead of relying on order. If it passes the linter then all is good. It doesn't matter as much for trivial and anonymous test-cases such as we have here. However, worth a thought. When the fields are more than 2/3 it gets more readable and more maintainable to name (i.e. `{s: "hello", n: 3, head: "hel", tail: "llo"}`). Also, I think golangci-lint (which is the linter used in production projects) will fail on default settings. I would put it as an anti-pattern, with a review leniency about only one/two fields in an anonymous struct.

Why cheap out on me? I'm paying for tokens, no need to shorten the examples. If a reader has gotten to read the top-level function's example, let it see all its contract at once.

Good use of `headRecovered`, from all the table tests we've seen, this is the most elegant to my taste. A good balance of the inherent complexity and the desired simplicity.

Also, I see this agent had named the struct fields of the anonymous slice definition - good job! I bet this is Opus.

In this version it is clearly visible that the two functions benefit from merging into a single test-case struct. Be it if running in two sub-tests (`TestRunesNotBytes/Head` and `TestRunesNotBytes/Tail`) or from a single loop with two explicit subsequent calls (one to each function).
